summary: The note surveys the growing role of herbal medicine in modern healthcare, covering its history, cost-effectiveness, efficacy evidence, safety and regulatory concerns, and integration into mainstream clinics. It draws on quotes from several experts and dated events between 2023 and 2024. It concludes that collaboration among clinicians and researchers is advancing integration despite ongoing regulation and safety challenges.
one_line: Overview of herbal medicine's rising role in modern healthcare, weighing cost, efficacy, safety, regulation, and integration into mainstream practice.
key_facts: Herbal medicine, also called phytomedicine or botanical medicine, uses plants' seeds, berries, roots, leaves, bark, or flowers for medicinal purposes and dates back thousands of years.
As of September 15, 2023, surveys suggested a significant portion of the population had started incorporating herbal remedies into their health regimen.
Dr. Emily Stone, a leading botanist and herbalist, says "many conventional drugs have their origins in plant-based substances."
The resurgence of herbal medicine is attributed to perceived efficacy, lower cost, and a desire for a holistic approach to health.

A study published November 10, 2023 by the Alternative Healthcare Economics Research Institute (AHERI) found patients who integrated herbal practices reported lower overall healthcare costs, including reduced spending on prescriptions and over-the-counter medications.
Health economist Dr. John Kessler said herbal remedies often require less processing and fewer resources to produce, but long-term savings depend on use under knowledgeable practitioners.
Critics argue herbal medicine lacks sufficient standardized clinical trials to establish effectiveness.

Dr. Lisa Hamilton, a naturopathic physician, cited a January 2024 study in which Ginkgo biloba extract improved cognitive function in patients with mild Alzheimer's; she spoke at a seminar on February 20, 2024.
Unlike pharmaceutical drugs, herbal supplements are not subject to the FDA's rigorous testing and approval standards.

Pharmacologist Dr. Mark Daniels warned on March 1, 2024 that lack of regulation can cause product quality issues and harmful interactions, and advised patients to consult healthcare providers before starting any herbal regimen.
The Center for Integrative Health in New York launched an initiative on April 10, 2024 featuring a dedicated herbal therapy department.
Dr. Nina Patel, Chief Medical Officer at the Center for Integrative Health, said "Integration is key to maximizing patient outcomes."
Medical curriculums are beginning to include courses on herbal medicine and pharmacognosy.
Dr. Sandra Beck, a research director at the NCCIH, said on May 15, 2024 that "It's an exciting time for herbal medicine research."
